blocks.prompt: The Dirty Snowball That Grows a Tail
blocks.text: A comet is a ball of ice, dust, and rock. People call it a dirty snowball. Most of the time, a comet is very far from the sun. Out there it is dark and cold, and the comet is just a quiet lump of ice. Then its long path brings it close to the sun. The sun warms the ice. The ice turns into gas, and dust comes off with it. The gas and dust stream away into space. That is the tail, and it can be millions of miles long. Here is the funny part. The tail always points away from the sun. So when a comet heads back out into the dark, it goes tail first.

blocks.prompt: The Snowball That Wakes Up
blocks.text: A comet spends almost its whole life asleep. Far from the sun, out past the planets, it is nothing but a dark lump of ice, dust, and rock. Most comets are only a few miles wide. You could walk across one in an afternoon. Then its long path swings it toward the sun, and it wakes up. Sunlight heats the ice. The ice does not melt into water first. It turns straight into gas, skipping the liquid step, and scientists call that sublimation. Gas and dust burst off the surface and wrap the comet in a glowing cloud bigger than a planet. Sunlight and the wind of tiny particles blowing off the sun push that cloud out into a long tail. Here is the strange part. A comet's tail does not trail behind it the way smoke trails behind a train. The tail always points away from the sun. So when the comet swings around and heads back out into the dark, it flies tail first. The closer a comet gets to the sun, the brighter it burns, and the more of itself it loses. Every trip costs it a little ice.

notes: Four parts: nucleus, coma, dust tail, ion tail
A nucleus reflects only about 4% of light
A coma can grow wider than Jupiter
Ion tails are blue and straight
Dust tails are pale and curved
Meteor showers are old comet dust

blocks.prompt: The Four Parts of a Comet
blocks.text: Every comet has the same parts, and only one of them is solid. The nucleus is the comet itself: a lump of ice, dust, and rock left over from the building of the solar system about four and a half billion years ago. Most are just a few miles across. Their surfaces are astonishingly dark. A comet nucleus reflects only about four percent of the light that lands on it, which makes it blacker than charcoal. The coma comes next. As the nucleus nears the sun, its ice sublimates, turning straight from solid to gas without ever becoming liquid. The escaping gas and dust swell into a glowing shell around the nucleus. A coma can grow wider than the planet Jupiter, all of it fed by a lump of ice you could walk across in an afternoon. Then come the tails, and there are usually two. The dust tail is pale and gently curved. It is made of grit pushed out by the pressure of sunlight, and it drifts along behind the comet's path. The ion tail is blue and arrow straight. It is made of gas that the sun has given an electric charge, and the solar wind, a stream of particles racing off the sun, blows it directly away at enormous speed. That is the rule worth remembering. Tails point away from the sun, not backward along the path. A comet leaving the sun travels tail first. The lost dust does not disappear. It stays in orbit as a long trail of grit. When Earth plows through one of those trails, the grains burn up in our air, and we look up and call it a meteor shower. The Perseids you can watch every August are the dust of a comet named Swift-Tuttle.

blocks.prompt: The Comet That Kept Its Appointment
blocks.text: For most of human history, a comet was bad news. A bright one appearing out of nowhere was read as a warning that a king would fall or a war was coming. When a comet blazed over England in 1066, the year of the Norman invasion, weavers stitched it into the Bayeux Tapestry with a crowd of men pointing up at it in alarm. Nobody thought to ask where it had come from, because nobody imagined it was following a rule. Edmond Halley did. Halley was an English astronomer and a friend of Isaac Newton, who had just published his law of gravitation, describing how the sun's pull shapes the path of everything around it. Halley wondered whether comets obeyed that law too. So he went digging through old records. He found something odd. A comet had been observed in 1531. Another in 1607. Another in 1682. When he worked out the three paths, they looked identical, and the gaps between the sightings were both about seventy six years. Halley made the obvious leap, and it was also the brave one. There had never been three comets. There had been one comet, coming back. Then he did the thing that mattered. He predicted its return for around the end of 1758. That was a genuine risk. He was staking his reputation on an exact claim about the future, and unlike an omen, a prediction can be proved wrong. Halley died in 1742, sixteen years before the test. On Christmas night in 1758, a German farmer and amateur astronomer named Johann Palitzsch aimed his telescope at the sky and found the comet almost exactly where Halley had said it would be. It has carried his name ever since. Halley's Comet returned in 1835, in 1910, and in 1986, and it is falling back toward us now, due in 2061. But the comet was never the real discovery. The real discovery was that the sky keeps its appointments.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko orbits the sun every 6.5 years
Rosetta flew 4 billion miles over 10 years
Philae bounced twice on landing
67P is blacker than charcoal
Its gas holds glycine, an amino acid
Its water carries 3x Earth's deuterium

blocks.prompt: Ten Years to Land on a Snowball
blocks.text: On November 12, 2014, a robot the size of a washing machine dropped toward a comet traveling through space at tens of thousands of miles per hour, and the engineers watching had no way to steer it. The comet's gravity was so feeble that a person standing on the surface could jump and never come back down. Philae fell for seven hours, touched the surface, and then, because its harpoons failed to fire, it bounced. It drifted for nearly two hours, bounced again, and came to rest in the shadow of a cliff where its solar panels could barely see the sun. It worked for about sixty hours and went silent. That sounds like a failure. It was one of the great successes in the history of space exploration, and the reason has almost nothing to do with the landing. The comet was 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko, a lopsided two lobed lump of ice and dust roughly two and a half miles long, shaped rather like a rubber duck. The spacecraft that carried Philae, an orbiter named Rosetta, had spent ten years and four billion miles getting there, slingshotting past Earth three times and Mars once to build up speed, then sleeping through the coldest stretch of the trip with nearly everything switched off. Why go to that trouble for a dirty snowball? Because comets are the leftovers. When the solar system assembled itself about four and a half billion years ago, most of the raw material was crushed into planets, then heated, melted, and rearranged beyond recognition. The scraps flung out to the cold edge were not. They have sat in deep freeze ever since, barely touched. A comet is a sample of the original ingredients, and Rosetta was sent to read the recipe. It read plenty. The surface of 67P turned out to be blacker than charcoal, coated in dust and complex carbon compounds. The gas streaming off it stank, in the sense that its chemistry included hydrogen sulfide, ammonia, and formaldehyde, a blend somewhere between rotten eggs and a horse stable. Rosetta detected glycine, an amino acid that living things use to build proteins, and phosphorus, another ingredient of life. Nobody found life out there. They found that the parts were already lying around at the beginning. Then came the result that stung. There was a popular idea that Earth's oceans had been delivered by comets, that our water arrived from the outer solar system after the planet had formed. Water carries a signature: the ratio of ordinary hydrogen to its heavier relative, deuterium. Rosetta measured that ratio at 67P and found about three times the deuterium in Earth's seawater. Whatever filled our oceans, it probably was not water like this. The measurement did not support the hypothesis it was sent to test. That is worth sitting with. A ten year mission, a four billion mile flight, an almost impossible landing, and one of the headline answers came back as no. In science, that counts. A hypothesis that cannot be told it is wrong was never doing any work in the first place. Rosetta finished on September 30, 2016. Out of power, its team steered it into a slow descent onto the comet, shooting pictures until the moment of impact. It is still there, riding a snowball around the sun once every six and a half years, alongside Philae, which was finally spotted in its crack a few weeks before the end.
